Our review of the RTX 2080 vs. GTX 1080 Ti & GTX 1080 considers all scenarios. The RTX 2080 FE goes through gaming benchmarks (e.g. Far Cry 5, F1 2018, Shadow of the Tomb Raider), thermal benchmarks, noise/acoustic benchmarks, noise-normalized tests, power tests, RTX 2080 overclocking tests, and more. Our RTX 2080 Ti Founders Edition review will go up today as well, within a few hours of publication of this main content piece.

Part of the piece is spent discussing the marketing surrounding the "RTX" branding, along with the lack of RTX support in games right now.

This launch reminds me of a couple in the past. The Geforce FX was released in 2003, and was the first GPU with true DirectX 9 support. That was a big deal at the time. The problem is that the Geforce FX was really shitty at handling DX9. It had the hardware, and could technically do it, but not with useful framerates. We didn't see a good DX9 card from Nvidia until the Geforce 6800/6600's came out in 2004.

There was also the Radeon HD 5000 series in 2009. Those were the first DX11 cards. DX11 was a big deal, because it brought things like hardware tessellation to games. The problem was that the 5000 series cards got really slow when you turned on all the DX11 goodies, in the few games that supported it.

We have an even bigger potential fail now, with the RTX 2080 and Ti. The way they've priced these relative to real world performance is so insulting to the consumer. This is the type of technology that won't be worth a shit until the 2nd or 3rd generation. This always happens. comments.text:
@djphllps  
As stated in this video, a lot of the upset reaction is due to the misleading marketing, information and pricing.

The reaction is more towards to the company and it's practices, rather than at the technology. Yes, the technology is fascinating and will properly be part of future PC gaming.

However, it's completely rational reaction to be disappointed on how this was handled. If the information and marketing would have been more honest and transparent, probably more people indeed would focus on the exciting parts of these GPUs- about what they can bring in the future.

However... it's like you'd buy a horse that can jump a little higher than your previous horse. 

But the guy who sells it you, speaks about it being a flying horse and asks a lot more money for it- and then in reality, you realize-  
"Oh okay this horse can jump like 20% higher, but it ain't flying, and I paid a shitload of more than I did for my previous 🏇"

And the guy only THEN tells you, "sorry bud, what I meant is, that the horses of this breed can MAYBE fly in the future, but right now, hey it can jump a little higher, so maybe you can just deal with that now and let's do business again in few years?"

- what do you think, after that kind of experience would you feel happy about that 20% increase for what you paid 50% more....or would you be happy about that maybe in the future, you can buy another horse from the same guy, and MAYBE it can really fly?

Yeah. I'd be pretty cynical after that. And that's why we aren't dreaming wide-eyed about the future of RTX. Because we feel ripped off, rather than grateful. And who can blame us?

If the pricing was bit more reasonable, if marketing was more transparent, IF THERE ACTUALLY WOULD ALREADY BE GAMES OUT THAT IMPLEMENT RTX WITHOUT LOSING 60 FRAMES, then maybe people wouldn't feel ripped off and disappointed in the industry as a whole, then yes, the reaction probably would be more towards excitement.

Disclaimer: I don't really like horses.

Why a 1080 ti vs 2080 is a better buy?
In terms of overall gaming performance, the graphical capabilities of the Nvidia GeForce RTX 2080 are very slightly better than the Nvidia GeForce GTX 1080 Ti Colorful Founders Edition 11GB.
https://youtu.be/jUM_eINGUl4
The GeForce RTX 2080 has a 35 MHz higher core clock speed than the GTX 1080 Ti, but the GTX 1080 Ti has 40 more Texture Mapping Units than the GeForce RTX 2080. As a result, the GTX 1080 Ti exhibits a 52.7 GTexel/s better Texture Fill Rate than the GeForce RTX 2080. This still holds weight but shader performance is generally more relevant, particularly since both of these GPUs support at least DirectX 10.

The GeForce RTX 2080 has a 35 MHz higher core clock speed than the GTX 1080 Ti, but the GTX 1080 Ti has 24 more Render Output Units than the GeForce RTX 2080. As a result, the GTX 1080 Ti exhibits a 33.2 GPixel/s better Pixel Fill Rate than the GeForce RTX 2080. However, both GPUs support DirectX 9 or above, and pixeling performance is only really relevant when comparing older cards.

The GeForce RTX 2080 has not been released yet, so any comparisons on this page are likely to be unreliable.

The GTX 1080 Ti has 3072 MB more video memory than the GeForce RTX 2080, so is likely to be much better at displaying game textures at higher resolutions. This is supported by the fact that the GTX 1080 Ti also has superior memory performance overall.

The GTX 1080 Ti has 36.4 GB/sec greater memory bandwidth than the GeForce RTX 2080, which means that the memory performance of the GTX 1080 Ti is noticeably better than the GeForce RTX 2080.

The GeForce RTX 2080 has 2944 Shader Processing Units and the GeForce GTX 1080 Ti Colorful Founders Edition 11GB has 3584. However, the actual shader performance of the GeForce RTX 2080 is 5299 and the actual shader performance of the GTX 1080 Ti is 7654. The GTX 1080 Ti having 2355 better shader performance and an altogether better performance when taking into account other relevant data means that the GTX 1080 Ti delivers a significantly smoother and more efficient experience when processing graphical data than the GeForce RTX 2080.

The GeForce RTX 2080 transistor size technology is 4 nm (nanometers) smaller than the GTX 1080 Ti. This means that the GeForce RTX 2080 is expected to run very slightly cooler and achieve higher clock frequencies than the GTX 1080 Ti.

The GeForce RTX 2080 requires 215 Watts to run and the GeForce GTX 1080 Ti Colorful Founders Edition 11GB requires 220 Watts. We would recommend a PSU with at least 650 Watts for the GeForce RTX 2080 and a PSU with at least 600 Watts for the GTX 1080 Ti. The GTX 1080 Ti requires 5 Watts more than the GeForce RTX 2080 to run. The difference is not significant enough for the GTX 1080 Ti to have a noticeably larger impact on your yearly electricity bills than the GeForce RTX 2080.
